key_facts: The Welsh Government has been working with higher education (HE) and further education (FE) sectors since September 2016 to assess the impact of Brexit.
Nine sector analyses were initially conducted, but more recent work by Cardiff University has influenced current thinking.
The Welsh Government is collaborating with HE institutions to develop preparedness plans for both 'no deal' and 'deal' scenarios.
Funding for European programs in HE and FE is guaranteed until December 2020 according to a letter from the UK Treasury.
There is concern that in a 'no deal' scenario, Wales would lose access to around 50% of Horizon 2020 activities currently supported by the EU.
Welsh Government has allocated £3.5 million to the Global Wales initiative to support international recruitment efforts for universities.
EU student applications to Welsh universities have seen a significant drop this year, attributed to changes in tuition fee grants and Brexit uncertainty.
Swansea University has demonstrated success in attracting international students despite challenges, serving as a model for others.
The Welsh Government continues to advocate for the inclusion of EU students in post-study work visa provisions.
A new regional skills partnership approach has been introduced to align training with employer needs, particularly in construction, manufacturing, and health sectors.
Welsh Government officials are engaged in discussions with the UK Department for Exiting the European Union, No. 10 Downing Street, and the Joint Ministerial Committee regarding Brexit transition.
Multi-annual European funding has provided security for HE and FE institutions, and its loss is a major concern.
The Welsh Government expects continued collaboration with the UK Government to uphold commitments on replacing lost EU funding for apprenticeships and other programs.
The National Union of Students (NUS) is actively involved in providing feedback and shaping policy responses related to Brexit impacts on education.
The Welsh Government remains committed to implementing the recommendations of the Diamond and Reid reviews for HE funding reform.
Regional skills partnerships are being developed to address potential skills shortages caused by Brexit, especially in rural areas.
Welsh Government has initiated a review of how FE is funded, aiming to improve responsiveness to employer demands.
£10 million has been invested in regional skills initiatives to ensure alignment with economic needs.
